newsitem.title: NORWAY: Nycomed redeems itself with merger.
newsitem.headline: Nycomed redeems itself with merger.

text.p: Norwegian drugs group Nycomed ASA appeared to have redeemed itself on Tuesday after almost two years of investor displeasure by merging with Britain's Amersham International Plc.
Scandinavian analysts gave the thumbs up to the proposal, saying it made good strategic sense.
"There are great synergies between product portfolios and on the sales and marketing sides. Nycomed can now become a global player in the life sciences business," a Swedish-based analyst said.

"I expect more mergers in this area and this means that instead of Nycomed being 10 or 15th in the running order, it's taking a proactive role and will be number one, two or three in this sector," she said.

Nycomed and Amersham said they would merge to form Amersham Nycomed Plc, a global group with a leading position in in-vivo diagnostic imaging agents and research supply. It would have a market capitalisation of 1.8 billion stg.
Nycomed's A share opened up almost 25 percent following the announcement, peaking at 135 crowns. By 1350 GMT it stood 22 crowns higher at 130 crowns.

Nycomed, formally part of the energy-pharmaceuticals venture Hafslund Nycomed ASA, is a niche player in the pharmaceutical industry and is a worldwide leader in the development of diagnostic contrast imaging agents for X-ray, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound and nuclear medicine.
It also supplies a range of generic drugs and other products to primarily European markets.
In 1996 the group booked an operating result after R&D costs of 1.34 billion crowns and a pre-tax profit of 1.17 billion crowns.
Analysts said the merger appeared to have been well prepared and looked likely to be approved by Nycomed's shareholders.

In November, 1995, Hafslund Nycomed was forced to abandon plans to merge its healthcare business with Ivax Corp of the United States due to lack of support by shareholders, who complained of not being fully informed of the deal.
Hafslund and Nycomed later demerged into separate listed companies.

Management of the new Nycomed group came under renewed criticism in June last year after it sent out a bleak full-year profit warning following stronger than expected competition in the U.S. contrasting agents market. Many analysts said the management had been slow to see the inevitable.

Nycomed CEO Svein Aaser told reporters that the company had informed its three largest shareholders -- the Norwegian state pension fund, Folketrygdfondet, insurer Storebrand and conglomerate Orkla ASA -- of the proposed merger before the announcement.
"The companies understand the industrial arguements," Aaser told a news conference.
"We can say the Nycomed mangement has redeemed itself. The merger makes a lot of industrial sense and seems far better thought out than the Ivax deal," said an Oslo-based analyst.

"But it is still comforting that Amersham's management has an excellent track record and will occupy a lot of the top jobs. Nycomed is definitely the weaker partner and Amersham the dominant one," he said.
But analysts warned that Tuesday's share price surge looked to have hit the top.

"I'm more neutral on this the higher the share price goes. A lot of the upside is already realised, 133 crowns is a fair price," said another Oslo analyst. "Don't forget there's also a dividend of around four percent. There may be another five or so crowns but otherwise I think the company is fully priced at this level."
--Tanya Pang, Oslo newsroom, +47 22 42 50 41
